name: Shapr3D
tagline: Touch and pencil driven solid CAD for iPad, Mac and Windows, built on a commercial geometry kernel.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: The interface is the part that looks copyable, and the interface is not the product. Underneath is a commercial B-rep solid modeling kernel doing boolean operations, filleting and NURBS surface intersection on degenerate geometry without exploding, which is the kind of code measured in engineer-decades, not in sessions. An agent can absolutely give you a browser modeler with sketches, extrudes and booleans in an afternoon, and it will feel fine until the first fillet on a non-trivial edge loop fails silently or your STEP export comes back as garbage in someone else's CAD. Add that the real workflow lives on an iPad with a Pencil, with pressure, palm rejection and sixty frames per second on a model with thousands of faces, and the gap stops being about features. Build the toy if you want to learn geometry. Do not expect to make parts with it.
coreLoopDIY: A local browser CAD toy: draw constrained-ish 2D sketches on a plane, extrude or revolve them into solids, boolean them together, and export STL or STEP.
requirements: opencascade.js WASM build, which is a large download and awkward to bundle
Willingness to read B-rep API docs written for C++ engineers
No iPad: this is desktop pointer only
whatYouLose: A battle-tested kernel: your fillets, chamfers and shells will fail on geometry that Shapr3D handles without comment
The iPad and Apple Pencil workflow, which is the actual reason most people bought it
Reliable STEP and Parasolid interchange with the rest of the CAD world, including supplier models and injection molders
Dimensioned 2D drawings, section views and anything you would hand to a machinist
Cloud sync, version history and working on the same file across three operating systems
moatNotes: The licensed solid modeling kernel is the real asset, and nobody is reimplementing robust NURBS intersection as a side project.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because CAD is one of the few categories where correctness is non-negotiable and almost impossible to fake. A note-taking app that glitches is annoying; a modeler that produces a solid with a self-intersecting face produces a part that cannot be manufactured, and you find out after paying for machining. People pay Shapr3D for a kernel that says no instead of quietly producing nonsense, for export files that open correctly in whatever the shop runs, and for a tablet interface that makes 3D modeling feel less like fighting a mouse. None of those three things are weekend problems.
notes: The sketch-and-extrude UI is a weekend build; the thing it sits on is not. The moat is a licensed commercial geometry kernel plus the decade of interchange and interface work that makes its output trustworthy to a machine shop.
prompt:
Build a local browser CAD toy. No accounts, no cloud, no telemetry. Everything runs on localhost and saves to the filesystem.

Stack, non-negotiable: Vite, TypeScript, Three.js for display, opencascade.js (the WASM build of the OpenCascade B-rep kernel) for all actual geometry. Do not hand-roll CSG on meshes. Three.js only renders triangulated output from the kernel.

In scope:
- A single viewport with orbit, pan and zoom, plus a small axis gizmo.
- Three fixed datum planes (XY, YZ, ZX). Pick one to sketch on.
- Sketch mode: lines, rectangles, circles, arcs. Snapping to endpoints and to the origin. Numeric entry for dimensions in a side panel. No constraint solver, snapping and typed numbers only, and say so in the UI.
- Close a sketch into a face, then extrude (blind distance, both directions) or revolve about a selected sketch line.
- Boolean union, subtract and intersect between any two solids in the feature tree.
- A linear feature tree in a sidebar. Click an item to select, delete the tail, nothing fancy. No real parametric rebuild: deleting mid-tree is disallowed.
- Fillet and chamfer on a single selected edge, by radius or distance. Wrap every kernel call in try/catch and surface failures as a plain message: 'kernel refused this operation'. Do not pretend it worked.
- Export: STL (binary) and STEP, both via the kernel's writers.
- Save and load the document as JSON describing the feature list, not the resulting solid. Reload re-executes the tree.

Out of scope, do not attempt: a constraint solver, assemblies, 2D drawings, sheet metal, surfacing, touch or stylus input, undo beyond a simple feature-tree pop, multi-user anything.

Practical notes: opencascade.js is a large WASM payload, so load it lazily behind a progress indicator and keep all kernel calls in a web worker so the UI does not freeze on meshing. Triangulation tolerance should be a settable number in the sidebar with a sane default.

Write a README that states plainly which operations are fragile and that this is not suitable for parts anyone intends to manufacture.
